/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs && python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:',len(r.pages))
print('Metadata:',r.metadata)
parts=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages):
    parts.append(f'\\n===== PAGE {i+1} =====\\n'+p.extract_text())
s='\\n'.join(parts)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(s)
print(s[:32000])
PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages):
    print(i+1, tuple(p.mediabox), 'images',len(p.images))
print(r.pages[-1].extract_text())
PY"

strengths: Addresses an important deployment problem: estimating performance without production labels. Combining importance weighting with score calibration is a practical approach that does not require access to the monitored model’s internals.

The evaluation covers 959 dataset-model cases and 36,557 production chunks across five tasks and five classifier families. PAPE achieves the best reported aggregate results on all six evaluation criteria, including accuracy MASTE of 0.99 versus 1.05 for importance weighting.

Using the same density-ratio estimator for PAPE and importance weighting provides a useful controlled comparison. The unweighted CBPE baseline also helps assess the benefit of adapting calibration to the target distribution.

The chronological evaluation protocol, repository link, and explicit discussion of concept shift, support mismatch, and finite-sample limitations are positive. The public-data experiments raise no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The central claim of supporting any performance metric is not established. Equations (1)–(2) justify expectations of pointwise functions, whereas F1 requires a nonlinear combination of confusion-matrix quantities and AUROC requires a ranking-based construction. The manuscript supplies neither the corresponding estimators nor their derivations, leaving two of its three experimental metrics insufficiently connected to Algorithm 1.

The theoretical guarantee assumes target-distribution calibration without controlling errors introduced by the fitted density ratios and calibrator. Equation (4), as written, also conflates expected absolute label residual with absolute conditional calibration bias; these differ even under perfect calibration. The population argument is useful, but its relationship to the implemented estimator needs a more precise treatment.

Reproducibility is weakened by missing descriptions of the density-ratio classifier, calibrator family and loss, weight handling, preprocessing, and random seeds. Algorithm 1 estimates ratios on the reference observations used to train the domain classifier without explaining overfitting control. A repository link helps, but the manuscript leaves consequential implementation choices unspecified.

The large benchmark remains confined to one census-data family. Temporal splits do not establish the assumed invariance of P(Y|X), and there are no controlled covariate-shift experiments or measurements of density-ratio and calibration errors to explain the improvements. The sample-size analysis covers only one selected evaluation case.

The statistical evidence needs stronger reporting. The Wilcoxon result is presented as p = 0.0 without specifying the test unit or handling dependence among chunks and models sharing datasets. Pooling all chunks also gives larger datasets greater influence. State/task-level summaries and confidence intervals are needed to assess the consistency and practical magnitude of the gains.

Originality is only partially established beyond combining existing density-ratio estimation, weighted calibration, and conditional-expectation arguments. The paper does not explain when this combination should outperform direct importance weighting. Its abstract also claims reliance only on predictions and probabilities, although Algorithm 1 requires reference and production features.
